Negligent describes a person (or their behavior) that fails to take the reasonable care that the situation requires — and because of that failure, harm, damage, or risk results (or could result).

In simple words: a negligent person didn't do what a responsible, careful person would have done — and that carelessness caused (or could cause) a problem.
The Big Idea Hidden Inside the Word

The most important thing to understand about "negligent" is that it is not about bad intentions. A negligent person didn't necessarily want anything bad to happen. They simply didn't pay enough attention, didn't try hard enough, or didn't care enough to prevent it.

This is what makes negligent different from words like deliberate or intentional. A deliberate wrongdoer plans to cause harm. A negligent person causes harm through carelessness, inattention, or irresponsibility — they just didn't bother to be careful enough when they should have been.

The word negligent always involves an invisible measuring stick: what would a reasonable, responsible person have done in the same situation?

If someone falls far below that standard — they ignored obvious risks, skipped important duties, or simply didn't try — they are negligent.

This is not a test of perfection. Nobody is expected to be flawless. It's a test of ordinary, sensible carefulness. When someone can't even meet that basic bar, the word negligent applies.

• A babysitter who leaves a toddler alone near a swimming pool and goes inside to watch TV is being negligent. She had a duty to keep the child safe, and she ignored it.
  • A chef who doesn't wash his hands after handling raw meat and then prepares food for customers is being negligent. Basic hygiene is a clear responsibility, and he ignored it.
  • A driver who sends text messages while driving is negligent. Every driver has a duty to pay attention to the road. Texting removes that attention entirely.
  • A pharmacist who gives a patient the wrong medication because she was distracted and didn't double-check the prescription is negligent. Her job required careful checking, and she failed to do it.

Notice that in none of these cases did the person want to cause harm. But they were all dangerously careless in situations where carefulness was absolutely required of them.
Negligent in Formal and Legal Contexts

The word "negligent" is extremely common in legal, medical, and professional settings, because these are fields where people have formal, serious duties of care toward others.

  • A doctor who misses an obvious diagnosis because they didn't bother to run standard tests may be called negligent.
  • A construction company that doesn't follow safety codes, leading to a worker's injury, is negligent.
  • A lawyer who misses a critical deadline for their client because they forgot to check their calendar is negligent.

In law, negligent behavior is one of the most common reasons people are sued. If someone's negligence causes you financial loss, physical injury, or other real harm, the law may hold them responsible — even though they never meant to hurt you.

Not all negligence is equal. There are different intensities:

Slightly negligent — A small lapse in care that a reasonable person might occasionally make, with minor consequences. Example: a waiter who forgets to warn a customer about a slightly slippery floor.

Negligent (standard) — A clear failure to take care that a responsible person would have taken, causing real harm. Most everyday and legal uses fall here.

Grossly negligent — An extreme, shocking level of carelessness, almost approaching recklessness. This is when someone ignores an obvious and serious danger in a way that shows almost total disregard for others' safety. Example: a truck driver who operates a vehicle without functioning brakes because fixing them "costs too much."

The adjective gross is often placed before negligent to signal this highest level of severity.
What Negligent Is NOT — Important Distinctions

Negligent ≠ Accidental
A pure accident can happen even when someone is being fully careful and responsible. Negligence implies that better care could have prevented the outcome.

Negligent ≠ Intentional/Deliberate
If you deliberately hurt someone, you are malicious or reckless — not just negligent. Negligent behavior is careless, not calculated.

Negligent ≠ Merely Imperfect
Making an honest mistake after genuinely trying your best is not negligence. Negligence is about falling below a basic, reasonable standard — not about failing to be perfect.
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

"Negligent" typically appears right before a noun, or after a linking verb like "was" or "were":

  • "The negligent contractor left the job site without securing the scaffolding."
  • "The court found the hospital to be negligent in its care of the patient."
  • "Her negligent attitude toward the safety checklist put everyone at risk."

You will also often see it in the phrase "negligent in (doing something)":

  • "He was negligent in monitoring the experiment."
  • "She was negligent in her duties as a supervisor."

Since you'll encounter the whole word family in real life:

  • Negligence (noun) — the actual behavior or quality of being negligent. "The accident was caused by negligence."
  • Negligently (adverb) — in a negligent manner. "The nurse negligently administered the wrong dosage."
  • Non-negligent — not negligent; used mainly in formal/legal writing to clear someone of careless blame.

If you ever need to recall the word fast:

Negligent means carelessly failing to do what a responsible person should do, in a situation where that failure causes or risks causing harm to others.

That single idea — carelessness in the face of a clear duty, leading to harm — is the entire heart of the word.
